summary: Georges Island Light, front light of the Halifax Harbour Inner range: lit 1876, burned 1916, octagonal concrete tower of 1917; Parks Canada island, lighthouse closed.

lens.note: 270-degree fourth-order Fresnel lens in the 1917 tower (LighthouseFriends). The 1913-14 Marine report records a fourth-order occulting dioptric lens, red, in place of the revolving catoptric light; NSLPS dates a fourth-order dioptric lens to 1922.

structures.note: first lighthouse; 21 ft (6.4 m) square wooden building painted drab, two fixed white lights; built by Thomas Halliwell for $1,300 (LighthouseFriends). NSLPS describes the first tower as 35 ft (10.7 m) high.
35 ft (10.7 m), built against the western side of the keeper's dwelling for a revolving red light; burned 1916 (LighthouseFriends, NSLPS, Rowlett)
octagonal concrete tower with cast-iron lantern room (8 ft) housing a 270-degree fourth-order Fresnel lens; Coast Guard list gives 16.4 m; Rowlett gives 16 m

structures.type: white wooden tower on the Dartmouth Exhibition building
structures.note: 70 ft (21.3 m); fixed red catoptric light, in line with the George Island light from 31 March 1903 (Marine report)
about 100 m from the Dartmouth exhibition building; rear light by 1920 (LighthouseFriends); Coast Guard list gives a triangular skeletal tower
still standing about 200 ft from the tower (NSLPS)

access.note: Island open by ferry from Halifax (Parks Canada; Ambassatours Gray Line) or by private boat. Lighthouse grounds and tower closed (LighthouseFriends; Rowlett).

events.note: Robert Ross, sapper in the Royal Engineers, appointed keeper 18 January 1876 at $150 a year
fog bell from Meagher's Beach placed in operation 1 April 1889 (LighthouseFriends); NSLPS gives 1899 for the transfer
two fixed white lights replaced by one revolving red light in a polygonal iron lantern (spring 1903)
square wooden tower built against the keeper's dwelling for the revolving red light
Dartmouth Exhibition building tower raised to 70 ft and lit 31 March 1903 as the rear light of the range

fourth-order lens replaced the revolving catoptric apparatus; the Marine table records a fourth-order occulting dioptric lens, red light (fiscal 1913-14; George Island row on printed p. 40, checked on the page image)
second lighthouse destroyed by fire; temporary red occulting light shown (NSLPS); provisional light until 1917 (LighthouseFriends)
octagonal concrete tower built and the present light shown; keeper's dwelling also built 1917
black pyramidal skeletal rear light built about 100 m from the exhibition building
a vessel (name not given in the casualty table as read) stranded on Georges Island, 29 December 1909; master not to blame, mate censured and fined $10 at Halifax inquiry, 14 February 1910
Sarah Radcliffe (London, official number 105182) stranded on the north side of the island, 23 March 1917; inquiry at Halifax 1 April 1917
army moved onto the island with an anti-aircraft battery (NSLPS)
island declared a National Historic Site
station automated two years after commercial power reached it in 1970
red stripe painted on the tower

corrections.why: The record's agency is truncated. NSLPS and the Coast Guard list give the Coast Guard as operator; Parks Canada manages the island as a National Historic Site.
The Coast Guard list gives the focal height of the front range light as 17.7 m.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: First light 15 January 1876 (LighthouseFriends). The present tower dates from 1917 (LighthouseFriends, NSLPS, Rowlett). NSLPS says the new light was lit 'early in January' without giving the year in that sentence. A Wikipedia lead gives 1919 for the first lighting of the present light; not cited.

LighthouseFriends: a fourth-order Fresnel lens installed 1913 (red light on the 1913 description). The Marine report for fiscal 1913-14 records a fourth-order occulting dioptric red lens (matched by column position). NSLPS: group occulting white until a fourth-order dioptric lens in 1922. The sources disagree on the date and the type.
LighthouseFriends gives 1889 for the fog bell's transfer from Meagher's Beach; NSLPS gives 1899.

LighthouseFriends and the NSLPS narrative give 1917 for the present tower and NSLPS says it was lit 'early in January'; NSLPS's own table gives 'Began 1918, Year Lit 1919'. The story gives 1917 for the tower and states the table's 1919.
NSLPS's text gives 1899 and its table gives 1889; LighthouseFriends gives 1889 (placed in operation 1 April). The story gives the LighthouseFriends date and the NSLPS text date.

LighthouseFriends quotes the Department's 1876 description as 21 ft (6.4 m) high; NSLPS's text gives 35 ft (10.7 m) for the first tower, the same height LighthouseFriends gives for the 1903 tower. The story states both.

notes_for_editor: Fact-checked 2026-10-28. Image checks: scan p. 142 (printed 135) shows the 23 March 1917 George Island stranding against the Sarah Radcliffe (London, 105182), not the St. Winifred: the St. Winifred name was misaligned in the OCR, so the story now names the Sarah Radcliffe and the St. Winifred is dropped. Scan p. 47 (printed 40, Nova Scotia works): the George Island row carries the 4th-order occulting dioptric lens, red light, in lieu of revolving catoptric apparatus. Scan p. 183 (printed 174, Nova Scotia keepers): the Ross, Robert row carries 'George Island Light and Fog Bell' and appointment Jan. 18, 1876. The 1909 casualty (scan 220, printed 218) is a narrative entry, 'Dec. 29 stranded on Georges island'; the vessel is not named in the story. The 1917 Halifax explosion and the Mont-Blanc/Imo inquiry (scan 73, printed 74) are in the harbour; no source read ties them to the island, and the story says so. Rowlett's Pier 21 view is credited there to Rip Irwin; the story cites LighthouseFriends and Rowlett for the closest/best view. NSLPS is internally inconsistent: the fog bell is 1899 in its text and 1889 in its table; the present light is 1917 in its text and 'Year Lit 1919' in its table; the first tower is 35 ft in its text and 21 ft in its table. Victor Matthews (1946-1964) and David Barkhouse (1964-1972) are named only as published sources name them, in their public role; NSLPS's personal memories of the Matthews and Nolan families are not used. Keeper S. B. Ross and J. Ross come from LighthouseFriends only. The Wikipedia lead (1919 for the first lighting) is not cited. The Manitoba George Island (Marine reports) is a different place and is excluded. Canadian units: metres first, with the imperial figure in brackets.
